lead: Sources are the parts of a circuit that push energy into it. An independent source fixes its own voltage or current, no matter what the rest of the circuit does. A dependent source fixes its voltage or current as a multiple of a voltage or current somewhere else. This difference matters because dependent sources model transistors, op-amps and amplifiers, where one part controls another. Phone chargers, UPI payment terminals and power supplies all use these ideas.
prereq: You need circuit elements R, L, C and their V-I relations for voltage, current and the passive sign convention.

sections.h3: Independent sources set their own value

blocks.text: An ideal independent voltage source keeps its terminal voltage fixed at V<sub>s</sub> volts. Its current is set by the circuit outside it. The source can supply any current, so its V-I line is vertical at v = V<sub>s</sub>. V<sub>s</sub> is the fixed source voltage in volts; v is the terminal voltage in volts. The symbol is a circle with + and − marks.

An ideal independent current source keeps its current fixed at I<sub>s</sub> amperes. Its voltage is set by the circuit outside it, so its V-I line is horizontal at i = I<sub>s</sub>. I<sub>s</sub> is the fixed source current in amperes; i is the terminal current in amperes. The symbol is a circle with an arrow. The arrow gives the direction of positive current.

An ideal voltage source has zero internal resistance. An ideal current source has infinite internal resistance. A practical source is an ideal source plus an internal resistance Rs in ohms. A practical voltage source is Vs in series with Rs; its terminal voltage falls as load current rises: v = Vs − i Rs. A practical current source is Is in parallel with Rs; part of Is goes through Rs, so load current falls as load voltage rises. See source transformation for the link between the two practical models.

A dependent source has a control port and an output port. The control port measures a voltage v<sub>x</sub> in volts or a current i<sub>x</sub> in amperes. The output port acts as a voltage source or a current source. The output is a fixed multiple of the control variable. The symbol is a diamond, not a circle, so it is not mistaken for an independent source.

VCVS means voltage-controlled voltage source. VCCS means voltage-controlled current source. CCVS means current-controlled voltage source. CCCS means current-controlled current source. The gain μ is a pure number. The gain β is a pure number. The gain g is a conductance in siemens; 1 S = 1 A/V. The gain r is a resistance in ohms; r is also called transresistance.

A dependent source is an active element: it can deliver power. A transistor small-signal model uses a VCCS or a CCCS. An op-amp is often drawn as a VCVS. The control may be far away in the circuit. Substitute the control relation when you write circuit equations; the full method comes in Unit 2, mesh and nodal analysis.

Question. A circuit has four dependent sources. (a) A VCVS has μ = 5 and control voltage vx = 3 V. Find the output voltage. (b) A VCCS has g = 2 mS and vx = 4 V. Find the output current in mA. (c) A CCVS has r = 10 Ω and control current ix = 0.5 A. Find the output voltage. (d) A CCCS has β = 20 and ix = 20 mA. Find the output current in mA.

items: VCVS: output voltage v = μ v<sub>x</sub> = 5 × 3 V = 15 V.
VCCS: g = 2 mS = 2 × 10<sup>−3</sup> S. Output current i = g v<sub>x</sub> = 2 × 10<sup>−3</sup> S × 4 V = 8 × 10<sup>−3</sup> A = 8 mA.
CCVS: output voltage v = r i<sub>x</sub> = 10 Ω × 0.5 A = 5 V.
CCCS: output current i = β i<sub>x</sub> = 20 × 20 mA = 400 mA.

blocks.text: Answer. The outputs are 15 V, 8 mA, 5 V and 400 mA.

examples.question: A circuit has four dependent sources. (a) A VCVS has μ = 5 and control voltage v_x = 3 V. Find the output voltage. (b) A VCCS has g = 2 mS and v_x = 4 V. Find the output current in mA. (c) A CCVS has r = 10 Ω and control current i_x = 0.5 A. Find the output voltage. (d) A CCCS has β = 20 and i_x = 20 mA. Find the output current in mA.
steps: VCVS: v = μ v_x = 5 × 3 V = 15 V.
CCVS: v = r i_x = 10 Ω × 0.5 A = 5 V.
CCCS: i = β i_x = 20 × 20 mA = 400 mA.
examples.answer: The outputs are 15 V, 8 mA, 5 V and 400 mA.

traps: Treating a dependent source as independent: its output changes whenever the control voltage or control current changes.
Dropping the gain unit: μ and β are pure numbers, g is in siemens, r is in ohms. Convert 2 mS to 0.002 S before multiplying.
Using a circle for a dependent source. The diamond is the dependent-source symbol; the circle is for an independent source.
Ignoring the arrow or polarity: a negative μ, g, r or β reverses the output polarity or current direction.
Forgetting internal resistance in a practical source: the terminal voltage or current is not the ideal value under load.

quiz.q: Which circuit symbol marks a dependent source?
quiz.a: A diamond. A circle marks an independent source.

quiz.q: Why does an ideal voltage source not fix its current?
quiz.a: It fixes only its terminal voltage. The external circuit decides how much current it supplies, so the current can be any value.

quiz.q: A VCVS has μ = 4 and v_x = 2.5 V. Find the output voltage.
A CCCS has β = 50 and i_x = 12 mA. Find the output current.
A student writes: g = 3 S and v_x = 2 V, so i = 6 mA. Find the mistake and the correct current.
quiz.a: The student changed amperes to milliamperes without converting. i = g v_x = 3 S × 2 V = 6 A, which is 6000 mA.

quiz.q: A practical voltage source has V_s = 12 V and R_s = 2 Ω. The load draws 1.5 A. Find the terminal voltage and compare it with the ideal source value.
quiz.a: v = V_s − i R_s = 12 V − 1.5 A × 2 Ω = 12 V − 3 V = 9 V. An ideal source would hold 12 V at its terminals.

quiz.q: State one difference between an independent current source and a dependent current source.
quiz.a: An independent current source fixes its own current. A dependent current source fixes its current as a multiple of a control voltage or control current.

beyond: Not for the exam. Circuit simulators use letters E, G, H and F for VCVS, VCCS, CCVS and CCCS, so searching those SPICE element names shows how the four models are entered in software. Transistor datasheets give small-signal parameters such as transconductance, which is the g of a VCCS. Op-amp datasheets give open-loop gain, which maps to μ of a VCVS. Search next for small-signal models and controlled-source SPICE elements.
